script.title: This is marble home: a simulation study of whether a humanoid robot can learn household chores from demonstrations, inside rooms generated by the World Labs Marble world model. Everything here was trained and measured on a laptop CPU.
script.worlds: We generated five rooms with Marble: a kitchen, a living room, a bedroom, a laundry room and an apartment. Their collision meshes become physics. What you see is the splat file, drawn as points. One caveat up front: the API reports no metric scale, so every room's size is an assumption.
script.pipeline: The pipeline is deliberately simple. A scripted expert with privileged simulator state generates demonstrations for a Fourier G R one humanoid. A small neural network clones them: it outputs a hand position increment and a grip command. Every policy is evaluated on the same held-out instances, with Wilson confidence intervals.
script.hero: Task one: clear the table. Three cups go onto a tray. On the left, the scripted expert. On the right, the learned policy, on the identical instance. The policy sees item poses and its own joint state, not pixels. Item by item, it gets there.
script.tasks: The same recipe with different receptacles: three laundry rolls into a tote, and two cups into a dishwasher rack. These are rigid body proxies. There is no door, no sliding rack, and no cloth.
script.results: Three training seeds, thirty held-out episodes each. Dishwasher: ninety-six percent pooled. Laundry: ninety. Clear table: seventy-eight. And on clear table the seeds range from sixty-three to ninety-three percent, as wide as the gap to the expert. A single seed would have told a misleading story.
script.findings: Three findings. First, action parameterisation mattered more than model size: on the same demonstrations, absolute targets scored thirteen percent, and hand position deltas one hundred. Second, the image policy was no better than a blind policy that never sees the cup. Third, diffusion needed at least five denoising steps and still trailed the plain network.
script.failure: Failures are informative. Here the policy carried the first cup to the tray and set it down 1 centimetre from its slot. As the fingers opened, the cup shifted to 4 centimetres out, beyond the three centimetre tolerance. Because the demonstrations contain only successful placements, the policy had never seen a miss: it drifted to the edge of its workspace and pushed against the scene for the rest of the episode.
script.heights: One limit we then tried to remove: counter height. The dishwasher policy trained at eighty-five centimetres scores 100 percent there, but only 25 percent across the four training heights and 2 percent on held-out heights. The scripted expert solves every height we probed, so the fault is the learned policy. Training on thirty demonstrations at each of four heights gives 82 percent on those heights and 89 percent on held-out heights inside the range. It does not extrapolate: 0 percent at 0.79 metres, and 27 percent at 0.94. One seed, one task.
script.limits: Limits. Policies see privileged poses, not pixels. The tasks are rigid proxies. The three main policies train at one counter height, and the height fix covers only the dishwasher, only inside its trained span. And Marble's scale is assumed. The next steps are perception, articulated doors and racks, cloth, and more heights and tasks. Code, data and every number are in the repository.
